t65x_fg1p1c: Most people get to some kind of forgiveness eventually, or at least out from under the resentment. But it doesn't come on a schedule ("Okay, it's been a year, time to forgive Dad"), and you don't need it first to be safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable or get better. Resentment does narrow what you can see, and it keeps your little one organized around the injury. Forcing it early just gets you an enlightened-looking performance while the wound goes underground.
t65x_fg1p1d: Will you ever forgive them? Maybe. A lot of people get there, or at least stop living inside the resentment. But nobody gets to put it on a schedule, and you don't need it first to be safe, or set boundaries, or get better. Resentment narrows what you see and keeps your little one built around the injury. And forgiving too early tends to turn into a spiritual act you put on for an audience (often yourself) while the wound goes underground.
t65x_fg1p2c: What can help is seeing how their history and pain, and what they were capable of at the time, shaped the harm they did. Given everything they'd become by then, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never processed. When you see that for yourself (not because someone told you that you should), forgiveness can show up on its own, and the rage that made them the one uniquely guilty person can soften into something more accurate.
t65x_fg1p2d: One thing that tends to help is seeing the whole chain: what happened to them, what they learned, what they could and couldn't do by the time they got to you. From inside all that, the harmful move was the only one they had. "Hurt people hurt people" is a cliché because it's often true. And once you see it for yourself, forgiveness sometimes just arrives, uninvited, and the rage that made them the villain of the whole story softens into something more accurate.
t65x_fg1p3ac: None of that makes what they did harmless, or means there was no other option in some abstract sense. It means punishing them can't reach back and give them the awareness or support they didn't have. What you can do is repair what's repairable and make a different response easier now. The harm is real, and accountability stays.
t65x_fg1p3bc: So the boundaries can stay. So can the legal consequences and the moral judgment, and the distance, for good if that's what it takes. You can understand how they got that way, hold them responsible, block their number, and forgive them, all at once. "I get how you became this" can sit right next to "and now I get why I can't count on you for this."
t65x_fg1p4c: Forgiving yourself works the same way, and if that one's stuck, forgiving other people tends to stick too. Own what you did and its impact (only yours, not what was someone else's). Let the remorse land, repair what you can, and then you're allowed to stop punishing yourself, with the responsibility still yours. Some harms take years. Living in resentment for good is its own trap, so come back to the question of how they got capable of it now and then, and let the understanding change how you feel when it's ready to.
t65x_le1p1c: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn't shown up.
t65x_le1p2c: So ask what has really ended, and what you're still trying to keep going. What isn't known yet? What is your little one scared will happen in the gap? ("Nobody's ever going to want me again" is a popular one.) And what small ritual, or practical thing, could mark the ending without pretending you know what's next? Don't grab a new identity just because not knowing feels unbearable. You can keep your routines, take care of your body, grieve what ended and stay with your little one while the next life takes shape.
t65x_le1p3c: Missing someone doesn't have to become another problem to solve. Sometimes the ache itself can be a cue for love. If love is there, let "I miss you" turn into "I love you," or try a simple wish like "May you be safe. May you be held in love." You can picture them, or just feel which direction the care is going.
t65x_le1p4d: That's about what happens in you, by the way. It doesn't depend on them getting anything, and it doesn't replace grieving or contact (your boundaries and the practical stuff still count too). If sending love starts making you compulsive, or a little unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." And maybe send some of that care to the part of you that's still here.
t65x_ba1p1c: Reparenting usually gets pictured as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and a relational injury can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the grown-up jobs for you at once: groceries, planning, doctor stuff, rides, your social life, reassurance, protection, company, or just being the competent person next to you. If you have someone like that when you're struggling, that's a huge blessing.
t65x_ba1p2c: Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they've been showing you, and try it yourself. Other jobs can get spread around (friends, community, professionals or services, routines, a calendar app). So which of those jobs could become more yours? Which are healthier shared? Which really belong in that relationship? The idea is for your little one to get reliable care through more than one door, while the relationship stays as precious as it is.
t65x_sh1a2: Some people have the opposite problem: it feels like they're connecting, and the contact is staying near the surface. A long meditation and then sleep (especially a second sleep, after you've already slept once) can open up much more direct stuff. If that night's dream carries way more feeling and need than your daytime session got anywhere near, that gap is a sign the session stayed near the surface, a sign and not a verdict. Ask what became available, and how you see it now. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, change the dose before you give up on the whole thing. Earlier in the day, or a shorter session, might be enough.
t65x_sh1c: Some people have the opposite problem: it feels like they're connecting, and it's all happening near the surface. A long meditation followed by sleep (a second sleep works best, after you've already slept once) can open up much more direct stuff. So if that night's dream hits you with way more feeling and need than your daytime session got anywhere near, take the gap as a sign the session stayed shallow. A sign, not a verdict. Then ask what's available now that wasn't, and how you see it. If nightmares start wrecking your sleep, change the dose before you give up on the whole thing (earlier in the day, or shorter).
t65x_sh1p1b: Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like they're connecting with their little one, and the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a few hours and then sleeping, especially a second sleep after you've already slept once, can sometimes open up much more direct stuff. If that night's dream has way more feeling and need in it than the daytime session ever reached, take the gap as a sign the session stayed shallow. A sign, not a verdict.
t65x_sh1p2b: Then ask what became available that wasn't before, and how you understand it now. If the nightmares start wrecking your sleep, or leave you less able to function during the day, change the dose before you change the whole relationship. Doing it earlier in the day, or keeping it shorter, may be enough.
t65x_lm1p1h: If nobody loved you very well as a child, "love your inner child" can sound like nonsense, the way "just relax" sounds when you're panicking. You might want the best for your little one, hug them in your imagination, miss them, and still feel none of that warm stuff people mean by love. So start smaller.
t65x_lm1p2f: Borrowing still counts (the way you'd feel about a friend's kid or your dog, say). But if picturing someone kind only makes you feel more threatened or lonelier, go smaller: what's the least cruel thing a decent grown-up would do for you right now? Maybe it's not calling yourself an idiot tonight. Do that. Nobody's grading whether you were loved enough. It's scaffolding, and the warmth can grow in on its own time, if it does.
t65x_lm1p3f: With the meanness out of the way, warmth has room to come in. And what people mention most is letting their guard down, on purpose, once the guarding part has had its say. If love has never felt safe, the ego can stand at the door like a bouncer who's been told "no feelings tonight," and vulnerability is the gap that lets one through. So the warmth may not be gone. It may be parked behind a cold part that's protecting something, and that part tends to step aside once it's heard.
t65x_lm2p1f: Then there's "No. I hate myself." Some people say exactly that when the love talk starts. If that's what you find in there, I'm not going to argue you out of it; it gets an honest hearing. But I'd hate to skip over the other thing. You chose to open this. Maybe you also chose therapy, or asked someone for help, or tried again after deciding you were hopeless. Something in you wanted something to be different.
t65x_lm3p1f: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Sounds intense, and sometimes it is. For some people, deep grieving turns into warmth, or into this full-body sense of being held by the universe. That's real as an experience, though it doesn't explain what the body is doing. And it can go the other way: somebody's kindness can make you cry about the kindness you never got, which doesn't mean the love failed. Go as far as you can while you're still present and choosing, and slow down when it starts to swamp you.
t65x_lm4p3e: If you're curious about any of this, follow the curiosity, no fake believing required. Read people from a few different traditions. Hang around people whose lives make you wonder what they found. Then check the fruit. Does their path make them kinder, more honest, steadier around suffering? Or mostly more sure they've got the right explanation?
t65x_lm4p4d: And sometimes care isn't what's missing. The whole horizon feels too small. Dinner helps, a boundary helps, one kind sentence helps, and none of it touches the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" That question deserves a real answer. What would have to be possible for being alive to feel worth exploring, and not just enduring?
t65x_ks1p1c: First, before anything else: if you might act on it soon, get another human being involved right now, and put distance between yourself and the means. A crisis line or an emergency number counts as another human being. This is for you if you're about to act, if you can't stop yourself, if you're badly disoriented or intoxicated, or if the means are right in front of you. If you're not sure whether you're about to act, treat it as if you are. None of this is my answer to whether life is worth living. It keeps the question open long enough to look into it.
t65x_ks1p2c: Before getting philosophical, make sure there's an adult in the room. If the part that wants to die feels like all of you, try the noticing from Noticing Counts, or the borrowed adulthood trick, and invite in any part that can watch what's happening. A part that can protect your body, or just put off a decision that can't be undone, counts too. If no part of you can watch right now, the questions below can wait, and the person you reached out to is your grown-up for the moment.
t65x_ks1p3a: Then ask: what is the self you want to kill? Is that self the same thing as your body? Why? Do you have the same body in dreams? What exactly do you expect your body's death to accomplish? If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?
t65x_ks1p4b: Buddhism doesn't teach that death is an off switch, or a free get-out-of-jail card back to the source. It teaches that repeated thought and intention shape the mind, that this keeps going through death and rebirth, that hell realms are possible, and that a human birth is a rare chance to understand suffering and end its causes. You don't have to believe that.
t65x_ks1p4c: But if you're still weighing your life against the opposite claim, look into that claim first (and if you're at the edge right now, the first step above comes before any of this). Near-death experiences and seriously studied rebirth reports can't give you reliable odds about death. What they can do is shake the certainty that destroying the body guarantees nothing comes after.
t65x_ks1p5b: You can see that momentum within this life, too. Rumination feeds rumination, and isolation can deepen despair. The more you hate yourself, the better your mind gets at it. Physical life keeps handing you redirections, though, like other people and things you have to do, and help when you reach for it. If the many traditions and the accumulating scientific evidence are right that the mind's causal process goes on after the body dies, killing the body may take away some of those redirections without taking away the suffering.
t65x_ks1p6b: And if losing everything is already on the table, what supposedly impossible change is still too frightening to try? Maybe it's a relationship, a job or a home. Maybe it's an identity, an obligation, a belief or a role you've been carrying. Those changes aren't free, and some can't be taken back. They're still smaller than dying, and you can make them once you're calmer, with help. Look into those questions, and into the life you've been afraid to change, while you still have a human body and people around to help redirect the path.
